questions.q: Why do many real organizations run multiple AWS accounts instead of one?
options: Separate accounts give each workload a hard boundary, so a mistake or breach in one (e.g., development) can't spill into another (e.g., production)
AWS requires a new account for every IAM user created
A single AWS account can only hold one EC2 instance
Multiple accounts are required to enable MFA
questions.explain: Separate accounts isolate resources, billing, and blast radius between workloads like production, development, and security.

questions.q: What is the management account's role in an AWS Organization?
options: It creates/owns the Organization, hosts consolidated billing, and is the only account that can perform certain Organization-level actions
It is just another member account with no special privileges
It replaces the need for IAM users in every member account
It can only be used for security auditing
questions.explain: Every Organization has exactly one management account, which oversees member accounts and consolidated billing.

options: A container that groups accounts (or other OUs) into a hierarchy under the Organization's root
An individual IAM user with elevated permissions
A billing statement generated monthly
A type of EC2 instance used for container workloads
questions.explain: OUs nest to form a tree structure, letting administrators organize accounts (e.g., Production, Development, Security) logically.

questions.q: How does a Service Control Policy (SCP) differ from an IAM policy?
options: An SCP sets the maximum permissions allowed across an OU or account (even restricting root), while an IAM policy grants permissions to a user or group
An SCP and an IAM policy are functionally identical
An SCP can only be attached to a single IAM user
An SCP grants permissions, while an IAM policy only restricts them
questions.explain: SCPs act as a ceiling on what's possible account-wide, including for that account's root user, while IAM policies grant specific permissions to identities.

questions.q: Does every member account in an AWS Organization keep its own root user and IAM identities?
options: Yes — Organizations adds a management layer on top; it doesn't replace anything inside an individual account
No — only the management account has a root user
No — member accounts cannot have any IAM users
Yes, but only if the management account explicitly grants that account a root user
questions.explain: Each member account retains its own root user, IAM users, groups, and roles exactly as covered earlier in the chapter.
